entries.title: Making Centipede ready for people
entries.event_semantics: 1981 anchors Centipede's production release as recalled by Bailey; the feature also reads her 2007 and later reflections. It is additive production history, not a birth-date biography.
entries.summary: Making, testing and teaching an arcade game.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; creator, primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: A descending insect was only the start of Centipede's development. In her Arcade Attack interview, Dona Bailey describes beginning with an existing hardware board already proved dependable. Graphics, play, scoring and sound arrived in stages. Other work would rarely be visible to a visitor watching a single game: test facilities, an attract sequence, coin handling and support for the cocktail cabinet. These were part of making an arcade product. The program had to behave usefully before someone paid, during a contest and when a technician examined it.

Bailey's account places a focus group and arcade testing before the production line began shipping machines in May 1981. Those encounters gave the team something different from its own familiarity with the game. She describes wanting an appealing, shimmering display and a trackball people would enjoy using, while resisting the assumption that she designed only for women. The intended invitation was broader. Visual pleasure and accessible movement were choices about how a person might approach the machine, rather than decoration after its rules were finished.

In her 2007 interview with Leigh Alexander, Bailey explains programming through syntax, structure and rules. She had liked reading and writing before discovering code, and did not describe her interest as a passion for calculation. That account widens the skills visible in the finished game. Assembly language could organise an image and an interaction as well as control machinery. It also qualifies a familiar biography shortcut: recognising a microprocessor did not mean that every question of game development already had an answer she could find in a book.

By 2007, Bailey was teaching writing and multimedia in Arkansas. She identified the cost of professional software as a barrier to learning and welcomed free tools such as Blender. Her teaching addressed a practical problem she remembered from entering game development: finding a way to learn when information or equipment was difficult to obtain. This is a later chapter, rather than another explanation for Centipede's success. It follows what a programmer did with accumulated experience, making technical practice available to students who had not yet reached an industry's door.

entries.title: Rules for people in the room
entries.event_semantics: 1983 anchors M.U.L.E.; a January 1985 contemporary interview also supplies a clearly identified comparison with the later Seven Cities of Gold. Historical bibliographic names are preserved in citations while museum prose uses Dani Bunten Berry.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; creator, primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: Dani Bunten Berry described a real-time stock-market simulation on an Apple as an earlier form of the idea that became M.U.L.E. In a January 1985 interview, she credited Electronic Arts with helping the team shape and communicate its work. Finding a publisher was part of finding a public. The computer could perform calculations, but the design still needed to let people understand events soon enough to respond. Bunten spoke about those human decisions as readily as the technology behind them.

The original M.U.L.E. manual gives food an unusual consequence: it determines how much time a player has to develop land. Energy supports production, and Smithore supplies the machinery needed for further development. A shortage therefore changes more than a number beside a resource. It can limit the next opportunity to act or alter what is available in the colony's store. The player across the room may possess exactly what another plan requires. Interdependence is written into the practical rules before anybody decides whether to behave generously.

The Tournament rules make private agreement an action. During a product auction, participants can coordinate button presses to enter a trading interval. Other buyers, sellers and the store recede while the selected players negotiate. The screen marks a change in who is allowed to make a deal. Cooperation can benefit two people and exclude another at the same moment. That ambiguity gives the social encounter texture: agreeing to help somebody is also a decision about everyone left outside the agreement, under the pressure of a running timer.

Bunten's later discussion of Seven Cities of Gold reveals the limits of discovery without guidance. The team gave testers a disk without explanation, then heard from people who could not work out how to leave their ship. A menu label that seemed natural to its makers did not communicate the action to everyone else. The lesson reaches back to the social design of M.U.L.E.: players need enough shared understanding to make meaningful choices together. Leaving room for surprise does not remove the designer's responsibility to make an action findable.

entries.title: Whose history becomes playable?
entries.event_semantics: 1987 anchors Méwilo's documented commercial release. The feature discusses a preceding career change and a subsequent Freedom project, using identified later interviews rather than invented period dialogue.
entries.summary: Tramis brought Caribbean memory into the choices of an adventure game.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; creator, primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: Muriel Tramis's route into games began with a decision about what her programming would do. In a 2021 interview, she recalled leaving military drone work because she could no longer accept its purpose. An introduction to Coktel Vision offered engineering and storytelling. Its director, Roland Oskian, allowed authors room to propose their own work. Tramis suggested a historical scenario drawn from the Antilles. Her technical training did not have to be abandoned; she redirected it toward a subject that she wanted people to encounter.

For Méwilo, Tramis worked with artist Philippe Truca and writer Patrick Chamoiseau, an old friend. In her CNC interview she recalled programming in Coktel's attic while compilation took hours. The game's investigation takes place in Saint-Pierre in 1902, before Mount Pelée's eruption. Those are two different timeframes: a twentieth-century setting within a game released in 1987. Keeping them distinct lets the visitor see the work as an authored reconstruction. The historical place reached players through pictures, dialogue and programmed decisions made by collaborators.

The next project, Freedom, placed the player in the position of an enslaved person resisting a plantation system. The CNC account identifies another collaboration with Chamoiseau and describes a strategy game about revolt in eighteenth-century Martinique. This change of position matters. The player is asked to act within oppression rather than watch it only from outside. That does not make a game an exhaustive historical record. It makes the choice of protagonist and permitted actions part of how its makers frame a difficult past for an audience.

In the later Xbox interview, Tramis connects these projects to questions about Martinique's place within France and to who gets to represent Caribbean lives. She describes making Black protagonists who could act on their circumstances, rather than appear only as passive figures. This is her account of her intentions, not evidence that every player understood the works identically. It supplies a way to read the design decisions alongside the software: a creator choosing whose actions matter and which history an interactive medium can ask people to attend to.

entries.title: Making a game belong locally
entries.event_semantics: 1989 anchors the company's documented first console launch in Brazil. The feature follows later localisation work through participant accounts; it does not assign unsupported day-level dates to adaptations.
entries.summary: Localisation connects software, characters and players.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; creator, primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: Tectoy's own history places its first Brazilian console launch in 1989. The work around that launch involved manufacturing and distribution as well as the machine itself. Its subsequent adaptations needed another kind of local knowledge: what a familiar character could do, what a reader could understand and where a player would seek help. The company became a place where imported software was reworked for a particular public. Those changes required practical labour and negotiations, rather than happening automatically when a foreign console acquired a Brazilian retail box.

Stefano Arnhold's account of Mônica no Castelo do Dragão makes one negotiation concrete. Tectoy licensed the comic character from Mauricio de Sousa's studio to adapt Wonder Boy. But Mônica could not simply inherit the original protagonist's sword. Replacing it with her blue stuffed rabbit, Sansão, reconciled the game action with the character's identity. The adaptation had to remain playable and recognisable at once. Permission concerned the behaviour depicted on screen, not just a logo or a translated title attached to otherwise unchanged software.

Alexandre Pagano remembered how that change became graphics. Characters were drawn on squared paper, then remade frame by frame with tools produced by Tectoy's engineers. His account describes finding a suitable adventure and working out which characters and story could be adapted within licensing constraints. A face was not a single replacement picture. It had to move, occupy the available space and remain legible across a sequence. The small marks on a television depended on people coordinating drawing, engineering and approval before players ever handled the cartridge.

Pagano also traced his own path from answering players' letters and telephone questions in 1990 to specialist game work and development. He recalled insisting that Phantasy Star would need translation to sell locally. The two activities met at the same problem: helping someone understand a game's possibilities. Support could reveal where players became stuck, while localisation could make a text-heavy adventure approachable in the first place. That connection gives the Brazilian story named work and practical decisions, beyond describing the region as a late stop for another market's hardware.

entries.title: What a port needs to survive
entries.event_semantics: 1995 anchors Heineman's account of making the 3DO conversion. A 2025 interview supplies a separately dated retrospective on archiving; no claim that every intermediate development asset survives is made.
entries.summary: Porting games and preserving their sources.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; creator, primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: Rebecca Heineman's introduction to the released 3DO Doom archive describes accepting work that was supposed to need finishing and optimisation. She then discovered that the promised near-complete version did not exist. Her account places the job in August 1995, with an October master deadline and roughly ten weeks of intense work. A port was not a compiler setting. Code, drawing methods, memory and sound all needed decisions suited to another machine. The gap between the promised starting point and the available material determined what she could deliver.

The archive describes several decisions made under that pressure. Streamed recordings replaced work on a music driver. Wall strips used the hardware's cel engine, while floors and ceilings stayed in software after another approach produced texture problems. These are explanations from the person who made the conversion, not excuses reconstructed from a disappointing frame rate. They identify where time and hardware behaviour met. A finished disc can conceal those alternatives; an account beside its source makes the accepted compromises available for examination rather than speculation.

In a 2025 VideoGamer interview, Heineman traced her archiving habit to assembling Interplay's anniversary compilation in 1993. When she needed Wasteland material, the source was not in a dependable central collection. She described obtaining a copy through contacts at Electronic Arts. Thereafter, saving snapshots became part of her practice, including work on MacPlay conversions. Releasing a game and keeping the materials needed to revisit it were separate tasks. The later port could become an occasion to preserve something that an earlier delivery had left vulnerable.

That interview also draws a boundary around the archive. Heineman said she retained source for the Fallout games through her Macintosh work, but did not possess all of Tim Cain's notes or early development files. She also distinguished possessing code from having permission to release it. A surviving snapshot answers a particular question about a particular version; it does not automatically restore the entire production history. Preservation therefore includes describing what was kept, recognising what is missing and establishing what may be made publicly available.

entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; creator, primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: ACMI commissioned More Than Just a Game for How I See It: Blak Art and Film, an exhibition curated by Kate ten Buuren. Its announcement placed Steel's playable work alongside moving images, photographs and installations by eight Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander creatives. The museum was presenting games within an ongoing conversation about representation, colonial archives and possible futures. A cabinet could therefore be more than an example of entertainment hardware. It could hold an artist's account of being on Country within a contemporary city.

In her filmed explanation, Jarra Karalinar Steel connects the installation to visiting arcades with her twin brother in the 1990s. The cabinet uses Blackwood Wattle and diamond motifs associated with Kulin and south-east design. A patterned floor brings her own visual language into the remembered arcade environment. These surfaces are part of the work, rather than a neutral container around its screen. Memory supplies a starting point, but the artist reshapes the space through materials and signs that locate the experience in her own cultural practice.

The Adventures of Dolly, made with Charlotte Allingham and programmer Peter Adams, lets its Koorie and Torres Strait Islander protagonist move through an alternative Melbourne. Steel describes a tram journey, conversations, errands and a community garden. Familiar places receive different names: Fed Square becomes Tanderrum Square, and the trams are Birrarung trams. Ordinary movement is the point. Dolly does not need to perform a spectacle of exceptional identity before she can occupy the city. The game's route makes relationships and everyday presence into things a player can encounter.

The exhibition's commissioning framework matters alongside that route. ACMI's announcement names five new commissions and sets them among other works that reconsider how First Peoples are seen on screens. It does not cast one artist or one game as a complete account of Indigenous experience. Reading Steel's installation in that setting preserves its specificity while allowing connections across film, images and play. The work belongs to a larger collection of distinct voices, and the playable form gives this particular voice a way to organise the visitor's attention and movement.

entries.title: Finding the game inside a limit
entries.event_semantics: 1980 anchors Game & Watch: Ball, identified in the Nintendo interview as released in Japan in April. A later Balloon Fight production recollection provides a separate example; no universal first-handheld or first-directional-pad claim is made.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; creator, primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: The Game & Watch developers' Nintendo interview makes a hardware limit countable. Ball used a chip able to control seventy-two display segments. Twenty-eight served the four-digit counter, leaving forty-four for the character and balls. These were shaped elements that could be switched on or off, rather than a freely drawn pixel image. Gunpei Yokoi and Satoru Okada were already making the prototype when Makoto Kano joined. The product's clarity emerged from choosing what those limited shapes should show, not from promising that the screen could depict anything.

The same conversation also keeps the calculator-on-a-train story at an appropriate distance. Kano says he arrived after work had begun and cannot describe its origin directly. Evidence appears when Yamamoto produces notes from an ideas meeting, including Chef. Colleagues describe many people offering suggestions, then Yokoi removing complications and concentrating the activity. The remembered method is visible in a working document and in their shared account of revision. It offers more to examine than a single scene of inspiration with every uncertainty smoothed away.

A separate Nintendo interview with Yoshio Sakamoto describes Yokoi proposing a floating sensation combined with fighting for Balloon Fight. Sakamoto drew and designed; SRD programmed the arcade version, while Satoru Iwata worked on the home version. The desired feeling came before a detailed inventory of features. Its realisation still depended on different people converting that request into pictures and behaviour. Crediting Yokoi as producer should retain those distinctions. An idea about movement could organise the work without being equivalent to drawing every character or writing each version.

Sakamoto's recollection of the bubbles is especially revealing. He thought a transparent-looking object would be impossible with the available graphics; Yokoi asked him to attempt it before refusing. Experimenting with the development tool produced a result that worked. The story does not prove that every limit can be overcome through insistence. It describes one moment when trying an image changed a designer's judgment of the machine. Beside the fixed segments of Ball, it shows another kind of economy: test what can communicate the desired effect before dismissing it.

entries.title: Ask where the decision came from
entries.event_semantics: 2006 is the Wii-era anchor. The feature compares the Wii Remote and subsequent Wii Fit development interviews; it does not claim that all conversations took place in 2006 or use Iwata's birth date as the technical event.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; creator, primary and institutional sources credited per card.
body: In the Wii Remote interview, Satoru Iwata asks Genyo Takeda what preceded the finished controller. Takeda describes small teams pairing GameCube software with dedicated interfaces, including the work that produced the Donkey Konga bongos and a dance mat. Another participant, Ikeda, traces his sensor experience through Pocket Pikachu and Kirby Tilt 'n' Tumble. The question turns a familiar object into a sequence of experiments by named people. A visitor can see that the controller did not arrive complete from a single instruction issued at the top.

Iwata then asks industrial designer Kenichiro Ashida about a turning point. Ashida explains the distance between his experience as a creator and as a parent with less time to play demanding games. Simply adding functions to another two-handed controller no longer answered that problem for him. The exchange preserves an individual reason inside a corporate product. Iwata's role here is also editorial: he asks for the change in thinking, rather than treating the final remote's unusual shape as sufficient explanation of how it came to exist.

The Wii Fit conversation exposes mistaken simplicity. Iwata asks when measuring balance entered the project, and hears two routes: hardware planners considered sumo wrestlers using two scales; a software developer found a posture method using a similar arrangement. Comparable prototypes did not require identical origins. The conversation then reaches rejected proposals and a team close to giving up. A product is easier to understand when its participants can describe uncertainty and disagreement without pretending that everyone recognised the answer from the beginning.

Later in that exchange, the board's width becomes the issue. Developers had concentrated on keeping a bathroom-scale-sized device compact and inexpensive, until exercise footage made a shoulder-width stance obvious. Iwata asks how the team experienced this change, even while Miyamoto sits in the room. The discussion allows conflicting instructions and practical frustration to remain visible. It is still a company-produced account, not an independent investigation. Its value lies in the explanation it preserves: the body, the budget and the size of an object were being negotiated together.
